outcomes.measure_name: Angular error of initial pointing direction (median per episode, group mean)
outcomes.higher_is_better_evidence: Their errors increased abruptly at the onset of the adaptation phase, and then gradually dropped again. Most importantly, adaptive improvement was more pronounced for young than for old subjects.
outcomes.operationalization: Group mean of the median initial movement direction error (between movement onset and peak velocity) per 50-s pointing episode, during the 15 adaptation episodes with +60° rotated visual feedback (episodes 6-20 in Fig. 1); late adaptation = final adaptation episode (episode 20). Also summarised by an exponential fit across the adaptation phase whose additive constant is the fitted asymptote.

sources.locator: Fig. 1, filled symbols in the adaptation phase (pointing episodes 6-20); last adaptation point = episode 20; triangles = young, squares = old
sources.quote: Fig. 1 Mean pointing errors of young (triangles) and old (squares) subjects before, during, and after exposure to rotated visual feedback. Open symbols indicate episodes where visual feedback was absent. Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.error_bar_evidence: Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.notes: Only source of group means/SDs for the adaptation phase; no numeric adaptation values are printed in the text. Filled symbols = visual feedback present (adaptation and refresh phases).

sources.locator: Results, ANOVA for the adaptation phase (between-factor Age, within-factor Episode)
sources.quote: significant effects were yielded for Age (F(1,22)=7.58, P<0.05), Episode (F(14,308)=41.14, P<0.001), and their interaction (F(14,308)=3.44, P<0.001)
sources.notes: Age comparison across all 15 adaptation episodes, not restricted to the final episode.

sources.locator: Results, exponential fits to the adaptation phase
sources.quote: An exponential fit yielded y=9.92+53.51×exp(−x/5.89) for young subjects and y=29.51+29.91×exp(−x/5.13) for old subjects.
sources.notes: Fitted-model parameters; the additive constants (9.92 deg young, 29.51 deg old) are the fitted asymptotic (late-adaptation) angular errors. No dispersion reported.

sources.locator: Results, additional ANOVA comparing pointing errors in episodes 20 and 26
sources.quote: we compared the pointing errors in episodes 20 and 26 by an additional ANOVA; the effects of Age (F(1,22)=13.78, P<0.01) and Episode (F(1,22)=7.79, P<0.05) were significant but not their interaction
sources.notes: Includes episode 20 (last adaptation episode) together with episode 26 (first refresh episode), so this age effect is not a pure late-adaptation contrast.

sources.locator: Results, ANOVA for the refresh phase (episodes 26-28, rotation re-instated)
sources.quote: ANOVA yielded significant effects of Age (F(1,22)=13.42, P<0.01) and Episode (F(2,44)=6.18, P<0.01), but no significant interaction.
sources.notes: Refresh phase = re-exposure after a five-minute break, i.e. a second perturbation block; listed only for completeness, it is not the initial round of adaptation.

sources.locator: Results, pooled analysis of adaptation magnitude A=(I−F)/I in an enlarged senior sample
sources.quote: The magnitude of adaptation in this sample was 0.49±0.21, and the normalized trail-making score was 1.78±0.55.
sources.error_bar_evidence: the magnitude of adaptation A after 12. 5 minutes of exposure as A = (I − F)/I ... 54 seniors aged 64.0±4.5 years
sources.notes: CAUTION: this value is for a pooled sample of 54 seniors that combines the present 12 old subjects with subjects from two previous unpublished experiments; no corresponding young-group value is printed. It is a proportional-improvement index, not the raw late-adaptation error of dataset 1.

outcomes.measure_name: Angular error of initial pointing direction without visual feedback (median per episode, group mean)
outcomes.operationalization: Group mean of the median initial pointing direction error during the five after-effect episodes of pointing without visual feedback that immediately followed the 15 adaptation episodes (open symbols, episodes 21-25 in Fig. 1); the first of these episodes is the first available post-learning measure. Errors are plotted as signed values that deflect negative relative to the near-zero baseline, so a larger recalibration corresponds to a more negative printed value.

sources.locator: Fig. 1, open symbols in the after-effect phase (pointing episodes 21-25); first after-effect point = episode 21; triangles = young, squares = old
sources.quote: Open symbols indicate episodes where visual feedback was absent. Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.error_bar_evidence: Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.notes: Only source of group means/SDs for the after-effect phase; no numeric after-effect values appear in the text. Note that pointing baseline without feedback (episodes 1-3) is also plotted with open symbols.

sources.locator: Results, ANOVA for the after-effect phase
sources.quote: ANOVA yielded significant effects for Episode (F(4,88)=66.84, P<0.001) and the interaction (F(4,88)=3.95, P<0.01)
sources.notes: The main effect of Age was not significant and its F value is not printed; only Episode and Age×Episode statistics are given.

outcomes.measure_name: Root mean square error between target and cursor in tracking (RMSE)
outcomes.higher_is_better_evidence: Clearly, tracking errors were higher during visual rotation; this increase was substantial in control subjects, and was followed by a gradual improvement, particularly for young participants.
outcomes.operationalization: Group mean RMSE between target and cursor per 50-s tracking episode (initial 0.5 s of each episode excluded) for the control subjects, who performed ten baseline tracking episodes with veridical feedback on day 1 and five tracking episodes with +60° rotated feedback on day 2; late adaptation = the last rotated tracking episode plotted for the control (thin-line) curves in Fig. 2.

sources.locator: Fig. 2, thin lines (control subjects), rotated-feedback episodes starting at episode 11; last plotted control point; triangles = young, squares = old
sources.quote: thin lines represent control subjects not pre-adapted with pointing
sources.notes: Only source of tracking RMSE values for the control groups; no numeric tracking values are printed anywhere in the text. Caption does not state what the plotted error bars represent. Note the x-axis of Fig. 2 is labelled 'pointing episode' although it plots tracking episodes.

sources.locator: Fig. 2, thin lines (control subjects), baseline tracking episodes 1-10 with veridical feedback
sources.quote: Fig. 2 Mean tracking errors of young (triangles) and old (squares) subjects before and during exposure to rotated visual feedback.
sources.notes: Baseline (pre-perturbation) tracking RMSE for the control groups, needed if a baseline-corrected value is required.

sources.locator: Results, ANOVA on above-baseline tracking error (Age × Procedure)
sources.quote: we calculated each subject's above-baseline error as the difference between the RMSE in episode 11, and the mean RMSE in episode 6–10, and submitted the outcome to an ANOVA with the between-factors Age (young, old) and Procedure (experimental, control). Only the effect of Procedure was significant (F(1,43)=144,09, P<0.001).
sources.notes: Concerns the FIRST rotated tracking episode (episode 11) minus baseline episodes 6-10, pooled across experimental and control subjects; the F values for Age and for the Age×Procedure interaction are not printed. Not a late-adaptation contrast and not specific to the control sample.

parsed.notes: Neither dataset has any numeric group means printed in the running text for the protocol outcomes: pointing angular errors (dataset 1, adaptation and after-effect) exist only as plotted means with SD in Fig. 1 (PDF page 3), and tracking RMSE (dataset 2) only as plotted means in Fig. 2 (PDF page 4, error-bar type unstated). Numeric text values in the paper concern the trail-making test (27.4±7.2 s young vs 42.5±6.9 s old, page 3; normalized 77.55±18.40 vs 103.93±16.26, page 4), reaction-time normalisation, and the pooled 54-senior adaptation-magnitude index (0.49±0.21, page 4) — the last of which is flagged as coming from a sample that merges the present seniors with two unpublished experiments. No aftereffect phase exists for dataset 2 (control subjects performed only baseline and rotated tracking), so no aftereffect outcome is listed there. No repository or 'data available from author' statement was found.
